segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of King Herod, magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: asking,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Where is the one who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star at its rising and have come to pay him homage.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When King Herod heard this he was alarmed, and all Jerusalem with him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and gathering all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Messiah was to be born.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They told him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “In Bethlehem of Judea, for this is what is written through the prophet:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: ‘And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you will come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Herod secretly summoned the magi and carefully ascertained from them the time when the star had appeared,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and sending them to Bethlehem he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Go and inquire carefully about the child, and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and pay him homage.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After hearing the king they set out, and there ahead of them went the star they had seen at its rising, until it came and stood over the place where the child was.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they saw the star, they rejoiced with very great joy.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Entering the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and paid him homage. Then they opened their treasure chests and offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And having been warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they withdrew to their own country by another road.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After they had withdrawn, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Get up, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and stay there until I tell you, for Herod is about to search for the child to destroy him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he got up, took the child and his mother by night, and withdrew to Egypt,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he was there until the death of Herod. This was to fulfill what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Out of Egypt I called my son.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Herod, seeing that he had been made a fool of by the magi, was furious, and he sent and put to death all the boys in Bethlehem and in all its surrounding district who were two years old and under, in keeping with the time he had carefully ascertained from the magi.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and great lamentation—Rachel weeping for her children, and she refused to be comforted, because they are no more.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Herod had died, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Get up, take the child and his mother, and go to the land of Israel, for those who were seeking the child’s life have died.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he got up, took the child and his mother, and entered the land of Israel.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there. Having been warned in a dream, he withdrew to the region of Galilee,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he came and settled in a town called Nazareth, so that what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled, that he would be called a Nazarene.

notes.note: The Greek word named a class of eastern (originally Persian) priest-scholars known for astrology and dream interpretation; it could also mean “magician,” as in Acts 13. “Wise men” is vaguer than the Greek and hides the link to star-watching that drives the story. Several modern versions also use “Magi.” The text does not say how many there were or call them kings.

This is Herod the Great, who ruled Judea as a client king under Rome and is generally thought to have died in 4 BC. He was known for his suspicion of rivals, which included executing members of his own family.

In verse 1 the plural of this word without the article means “the east.” Here and in verse 9 it is singular with the article, which most scholars now take as the astronomical term for a star’s rising above the horizon. “In the east” remains possible and is kept by some versions.

The verb means to prostrate oneself in reverence, and what it implies depends on the recipient. Here foreign visitors honor a newborn king, and verse 11 states the falling down separately, so “pay homage” is used in verses 2, 8 and 11. Translations are divided: NRSV has “pay homage,” while KJV, NIV and ESV have “worship,” and many readers see Matthew hinting at more than royal honor.

Herod is asking about a title, the anointed king Israel expected, not using a name. “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader where “Christ” can sound like a surname. Several modern translations make the same choice in passages like this one.

The quotation is from Micah 5:2, with the final line about shepherding God’s people echoing 2 Samuel 5:2, words spoken to David. Matthew’s wording differs from both the Hebrew and the Greek Old Testament, which call Bethlehem small among the clans of Judah; here its littleness is denied because of the ruler who comes from it.

notes.phrase: “Out of Egypt I called my son.”
notes.note: The words are from Hosea 11:1, where “my son” is Israel brought out of Egypt in the exodus. Matthew presents Jesus as retracing Israel’s story. “Son” is left lowercase so that the quotation keeps both its original reference and Matthew’s application.

The Greek noun is masculine plural, which can mean “boys” specifically or “children” of both sexes. Since Herod is hunting a male rival, most modern translations and commentators understand “boys.” The KJV has “children.”

The quotation is Jeremiah 31:15. Rachel, wife of Jacob and a mother of Israel, was by tradition buried near Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19), and Ramah was a town north of Jerusalem associated with the deportation of exiles to Babylon (Jeremiah 40:1). Jeremiah pictures her mourning the exiles, and Matthew applies the image to the mothers of Bethlehem.

notes.phrase: those who were seeking the child’s life have died
notes.note: The wording, including the plural “those” when only Herod has died, closely echoes Exodus 4:19, where God tells Moses to return to Egypt because those who sought his life are dead. The echo is one of several parallels this chapter draws between Jesus and Moses.

At Herod’s death his kingdom was divided among his sons. Archelaus received Judea with the lesser title of ethnarch and was removed by Rome in AD 6 after complaints about his rule. Galilee went to his brother Herod Antipas.

notes.phrase: that he would be called a Nazarene
notes.traditional: He shall be called a Nazarene
notes.note: No Old Testament passage contains these words, and Matthew speaks of “the prophets” in the plural without his usual “saying,” so the clause is rendered here as a summary, not a direct quotation. What he has in mind is disputed: common proposals are a wordplay on the Hebrew for “branch” in Isaiah 11:1, an allusion to the Nazirite of Judges 13:5, or the general prophetic theme of a despised servant. The Greek form is strictly “Nazorean,” which Matthew plainly connects with Nazareth.

candidates.reason: Matthew 2 uses it for eastern astrologer-priests, but Acts 13:6, 8 uses it for a sorcerer, so the split between “magi” and “magician” needs one ruling.

candidates.rendering: left untranslated in narration; “there” in verse 9
candidates.reason: It occurs some two hundred times, and translators vary between “behold,” “look,” “suddenly” and omission, so a consistent policy is needed for narrative and for speech.
It recurs throughout the Gospels and Acts, and versions vary between “scribes,” “teachers of the law” and “experts in the law”; a modern reader may take “scribe” to mean a copyist.
It recurs in Matthew, Luke, John and Acts alongside Mark’s Ναζαρηνός, and translations vary between “Nazarene,” “Nazorean” and “of Nazareth.”
Matthew’s repeated fulfillment formula (“to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet”) should be worded identically across chapters so readers can recognize it.

warnings: Verse 11: προσκυνέω is not rendered with a register form (worship; bow down before; pay homage; bow in worship) and has no register-exception note.
